text: I remember the moment I hit the wall with the hammer to start the renovation. And then just a tiny little piece of plaster came off, just crumbling and falling into dust, very gently. And I thought wow, and then hit it again. I did think that it was going to be quite violent and tough. And instead it was just crumbly. And that was the beginning of the whole process, which I had imagined was very, very simple. I just think: I'm going to knock down the wall, I'm going to paint everything in white, I'm going to put some shelves. I have all these books that are all over the place. I'm going to make it look nice. But I did not imagine the whole dust. I did not imagine that it would take so long. I did not imagine that there would be so many wires that are all very old and brittle. I did not imagine that behind the wall there were some pieces of newspapers from 1962, just inserted in there. And I did not imagine that I would be living for weeks in one room, eating just cereal next to the kettle. With all my stuff just stacked on top of each other and moving every time I move my body. But it became very interesting, because renovation is such a very deep process. It is not creating, it is just opening. And then everything that's behind the wall just comes out. The wallpaper, the plaster, the bricks. Some very tiny little scratches on the wood, the beams. With some letters and the date. I really felt like I was uncovering a very long history of people that were living in this very small space. And they were trying to make it beautiful, they were trying to repair it, to change it, to make it their own. And I really love that. I love to learn and to discover something. And then there was the very annoying part of the renovation, of the demolition. That's the part I hated the most. When the guy was coming every two or three weeks. And then just disappearing for a week, and then coming back with a new estimate. Or the tiles that I ordered were not the right color. Instead of being sage green, they were this super ugly green. And then the dust, the dust everywhere. In my coffee, in my mouth, in my dreams. And I was sleeping just on a mattress in the middle of the living room, surrounded by the beams. The exposed beams that were just like ribs of a skeleton. And I really thought, wow, it's awful. And I don't even know if I'm going to finish it. And yet, there were these very, very small moments. I remember once, when we knocked down the wall between the kitchen and the living room, and suddenly the light was coming in differently. Just making this super beautiful pattern on the floor and on the wall. And it felt bigger, the space. I don't know how to explain it, but it just felt bigger. And one of the neighbors came and said, "Oh, you're letting the apartment breathe." And I really love that. I love this idea of breathe. And then, very near the end, I just sat down on the floor. With the lamp just without the lampshade, all the paint cans that are half empty around me, and I thought, wow, I'm not in a hurry anymore. I really like it. It's not complete, but it's fine. The baseboards are missing, the door of the closet is leaning on the wall. But I feel at home. It is not a construction site anymore, it's a home. And I really love this distinction between house and home. And you can renovate a house and it's not a home. And this is the difference that I really learned. And then the last weeks, just the whole renovation to finish, was just paint samples, buying the hardware. And just all these little little things that look very small, but actually they're really big. And learning to accept that the floor is not straight, that the wall is not exactly perfect. That one corner is very weird. That there is still some old wall that's just there. That I couldn't take it down. But it's very nice to see just these pieces of old bricks next to the new cabinets. Or these lights that hang from the ceiling. That still have the trace of the previous one. It's not perfect, but it's nice. It's very authentic. And then, now, every morning, I wake up and I walk in the kitchen. And I love the light that comes in and touches the counters. And it's very nice, very warm. And I still see some little pieces of plaster everywhere, some dust. I still see this little scratch behind the drywall that we put. But I know that it's there. And I really love it. I really do.
